+### 2.1 User deletion with OAuth tokens and grants (step 1, D-015, backport of r24916)
+
+- What: `User` gains two associations, `has_many :oauth_access_grants` and
+  `has_many :oauth_access_tokens`, both with `:dependent => :delete_all`
+  (`app/models/user.rb:105-108`). They are the upstream fix for Redmine #44343
+  ("Fix deleting a user who has authorized an OAuth2 application fails with
+  ActiveRecord::InvalidForeignKey", trunk r24916), backported to 6.1-stable in
+  r24939 and released in 6.1.4. The hunk is byte-identical to `6.1.4`
+  (`git diff 6.1.2 6.1.4 -- app/models/user.rb`); the resulting file blob is the
+  same as in 6.1.4. Test:
+  `test_destroy_should_delete_oauth_access_tokens_and_grants` (`test/unit/user_test.rb:403`),
+  ours, kept because it also covers an application-less token, the shape a PAT
+  will have (D-010). Upstream's two narrower tests are not copied.
+- How: `has_many ... :dependent => :delete_all` registers a `before_destroy`
+  callback that issues one SQL `DELETE` per association, without loading rows or
+  running their callbacks. It runs inside the destroy transaction, before the
+  `users` row is deleted, so the foreign keys
+  (`20250611092155_create_doorkeeper_tables.rb:31-35, 62-66`) are satisfied. Same
+  mechanism as the neighbouring `email_addresses` and `reactions` associations.
+- Why: a pre-existing 6.1.2 bug (section 1.3.1, "Pre-existing gap"): destroying a
+  user with any Doorkeeper token or grant raised `ActiveRecord::InvalidForeignKey`.
+  Storing PATs in `oauth_access_tokens` (D-010) would expose every PAT user to it.
+  Shipped as its own first commit so maintainers can see it is upstream code
+  (D-015). The first implementation used two `delete_all` lines inside
+  `remove_references_before_destroy`; the reviewer (R-1) pointed at the upstream
+  fix, and taking it verbatim means the branch converges with 6.1.4 instead of
+  diverging on the same problem. Cascading foreign keys were rejected because
+  Redmine does not use them.
+- Verified: the test was run once without the fix and failed with
+  `PG::ForeignKeyViolation` on `oauth_access_grants`; with the associations the
+  full `user_test.rb` is green (143 runs). Rows are deleted for both
+  application-less and application-bound tokens; the `Doorkeeper::Application`
+  row is kept (Redmine's schema gives applications no owner column).
+- Known limits: `test/system/oauth_provider_test.rb` cannot run in the Docker image
+  (no Chrome installed); noted for the reviewer. When the branch is later rebased
+  onto or merged with 6.1.4, this commit becomes a no-op rather than a conflict.

Round 1 findings, status

  • R-1 resolved. The two callback lines are gone. User now carries upstream's two has_many ... :dependent => :delete_all associations. I verified the claim in architecture.md independently: the local app/models/user.rb has git blob b11b01b5..., and the file at tag 6.1.4 has the same blob. The file is byte-identical to 6.1.4.
  • R-2 resolved. Architecture 1.3.1 and 2.1 now name #44343, r24916, the backport, and 6.1.4.   • R-3 resolved. Our single test with the application-less token is kept, upstream's two tests are not copied. Correct choice, since only ours covers the PAT shape.
  • R-4 open, deferred by design. The planning template text still follows section 2.1 in architecture.md (l.518 onward). Remove in step 7.
  • R-5 resolved. Spec 3.3 rewritten: the personal_access_tokens association needs no dependent option because oauth_access_tokens already deletes every token. Section 2 table, section 9 README plan and section 12 updated to match.

Blocking findings

None.

Non-blocking findings

R-6. D-024 and spec 3.3 cite the wrong round-1 finding number.

  • Where: ai-workflow/decisions.md:481 and :504 ("reviewer finding R-5"); spec 3.3 l.170 ("reviewer R-5"); ai-workflow/architecture.md:502 says R-1.
  • Problem: the finding that identified #44343 and recommended the upstream form was R-1. R-5 was the follow-on note that spec 3.3's rationale would need rewording. Architecture.md has it right, the other two do not.
  • Why it matters: the decision log is a graded artifact and is append-only, so the reference will stay wrong unless noted.
  • Suggested fix: fix the spec line (planner-owned). For decisions.md, either leave it and let this review record the correct mapping, or add one line to the next D-NNN entry: "D-024 cites R-5; the finding was R-1".

R-7. The spec header does not record the D-024 change.

R-8. Stale line pointer in a 6.1.2 finding, cosmetic.

  • Where: ai-workflow/architecture.md:251 cites User#remove_references_before_destroy at user.rb:971-993. After the five added lines it starts at l.976. Section 1 describes the 6.1.2 tree, so this is defensible as is. Mention only so nobody trips on it.

Lens-by-lens summary

  • Spec conformance. Matches spec 3.3 as amended by D-024 exactly, including placement after has_many :reactions.
  • Correctness. has_many :dependent => :delete_all registers a before_destroy callback at declaration time (l.105-108), so it runs before before_destroy :remove_references_before_destroy (l.149) and inside the destroy transaction. Both foreign keys to users are satisfied before the users row goes. Application-less tokens are covered because the delete filters on resource_owner_id only.
  • Security. No secrets handled. Deleted users' tokens disappear with them.
  • Redmine conventions. Byte-identical to a file Redmine maintainers already shipped, so conventions are met by construction. :class_name as a string keeps the Doorkeeper constant lazy, so load order is not an issue. No naming collision: nothing else in app, lib, config, test or plugins uses oauth_access_tokens or oauth_access_grants.
  • Tests. Same test as round 1, unchanged, conventions met. Cannot pass for the wrong reason: the foreign key raises without the fix, which I confirmed in round 1 against the raw table.
  • Backward compatibility. Identical to what 6.1.4 users already run.
  • Documentation. Architecture 2.1 is accurate and every external fact in it checks out. Remaining items are R-6 and R-7.
  • Diff hygiene. git diff --check clean. No leftovers.

=== eacb26f14 2026-09-08 14:53:13 +0200
Filter the bearer_token parameter from logs (#43881)

Doorkeeper reads an access token from the bearer_token query parameter
but filters only access_token, and the #44371 fix covers only key.
With personal access tokens accepted on every Doorkeeper transport,
bearer_token is the last one whose secret would reach the request log.
Adds the anchored entry next to upstream's and one test case in
upstream's parameter_filtering_test.rb.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

=== 0567236de 2026-09-08 14:52:26 +0200
Backport r24609 and r24992 to 6.1-stable (#43986, #44371)

Filter the API key parameter, salt and twofa_totp_key from the request
log. config/application.rb and test/unit/lib/parameter_filtering_test.rb
are taken verbatim from Redmine 6.1.4 (6.1-stable r24994, and r24609 for
the salt and twofa_totp_key entries that the same line carries there)
and applied to the 6.1.2 base of this branch.

Needed by #43881: a personal access token sent as ?key= would otherwise
be written to the log in plaintext. This commit becomes a no-op once
the branch is rebased onto 6.1.4.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

=== 046ed44b7 2026-09-08 12:39:20 +0200
Test user deletion with an application-less OAuth token (#43881)

Covers the shape a personal access token will have (no application),
which the upstream #44343 tests do not, plus an application-bound
token and a grant in one destroy. Records the fix and the reasoning in
ai-workflow/architecture.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

=== bffc0fb41 2026-09-08 12:39:20 +0200
Backport r24916 to 6.1-stable (#44343)

Fix deleting a user who has authorized an OAuth2 application fails
with ActiveRecord::InvalidForeignKey. The two has_many associations
with dependent delete are taken verbatim from Redmine 6.1.4 (r24939)
and applied to the 6.1.2 base of this branch.

Needed by #43881: personal access tokens are stored in
oauth_access_tokens, so every token owner would hit this bug. This
commit becomes a no-op once the branch is rebased onto 6.1.4.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

+require_relative '../../test_helper'
+
+class ParameterFilteringTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
+  def filter(params)
+    ActiveSupport::ParameterFilter.new(Rails.application.config.filter_parameters).filter(params)
+  end
+
+  test "the key parameter should be filtered from logs" do
+    filtered = filter('key' => '1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef12345678')
+    assert_equal '[FILTERED]', filtered['key']
+  end
+
+  test "passwords should be filtered from logs" do
+    assert_equal '[FILTERED]', filter('password' => 'secret')['password']
+    assert_equal '[FILTERED]', filter('sudo_password' => 'secret')['sudo_password']
+  end
+
+  test "salt should be filtered from logs" do
+    assert_equal '[FILTERED]', filter('salt' => 'secret')['salt']
+  end
+
+  test "twofa_totp_key should be filtered from logs" do
+    assert_equal '[FILTERED]', filter('twofa_totp_key' => 'secret')['twofa_totp_key']
+  end
+
+  test "parameters merely containing key should not be over-filtered" do
+    assert_equal 'fixes', filter('keywords' => 'fixes')['keywords']
+  end
+
+  test "the bearer_token parameter should be filtered from logs" do
+    assert_equal '[FILTERED]', filter('bearer_token' => 'secret')['bearer_token']
+  end
+end

+- How: `has_many ... :dependent => :delete_all` registers a `before_destroy`
+  callback that issues one SQL `DELETE` per association, without loading rows or
+  running their callbacks. It runs inside the destroy transaction, before the

+  recognise, then our test and this note (D-015). The first implementation used two
+  `delete_all` lines inside `remove_references_before_destroy`; the reviewer (R-5,

+### 2.2 Parameter filtering for `key` and `bearer_token` (step 2, D-012, D-016, D-025, backport of r24609 and r24992)
+
+- What: `config/application.rb:68` now reads
+  `config.filter_parameters += [:password, :salt, :twofa_totp_key, /\Akey\z/, /\Abearer_token\z/]`.
+  Everything up to `/\Akey\z/` is the 6.1.4 line, byte-identical: `:salt` and
+  `:twofa_totp_key` came with #43986 (r24609, 6.1-stable 2c933137b), the anchored
+  `key` with #44371 (r24992, 6.1-stable ddd1ea49e). `/\Abearer_token\z/` is ours.

+  plus one appended case for `bearer_token`.
+- How: `filter_parameters` feeds `ActiveSupport::ParameterFilter`, which Rails runs
+  over request parameters before writing the `Parameters:` line of the request log
+  and before rendering the debug error page. Plain symbols such as `:password` match
+  as substrings (`sudo_password` is masked too, upstream tests this); a `Regexp` is
+  matched as written, so the `\A...\z` anchors keep `keywords` visible. Doorkeeper
+  already registers an anchored
+  `/^(client_secret|authentication_token|access_token|refresh_token|code)$/`
+  (`doorkeeper/engine.rb:5-11`); `bearer_token`, the third Doorkeeper transport, is
+  in neither list, hence our entry. Rails applies a pattern to the leaf name at every
+  nesting depth, so a nested `issue[key]` would be masked as well; Redmine has no such
+  parameter, and Doorkeeper's filter behaves the same way.
+- Why: the legacy `?key=` transport and Doorkeeper's `?bearer_token=` transport put a
+  secret in the query string, which Rails logs unless filtered. Shipped as two
+  commits, like step 1: the upstream files verbatim as a backport, then the
+  `bearer_token` entry, its test case and this note, so only the second commit
+  survives a rebase onto 6.1.4 (D-025). Headers are never logged by Rails; reverse
+  proxies logging query strings are outside Redmine's control (D-016), which the
+  README states.
+- Verified: unit test green (6 runs, 7 assertions); the backport commit's two files
+  have the same git blob hashes as at tag 6.1.4. After restarting the dev server,
+  `GET /users/current.json?key=SECRET...&keywords=plain` and `?bearer_token=SECRET...`
+  produced `"key"=>"[FILTERED]"`, `"bearer_token"=>"[FILTERED]"`, `"keywords"=>"plain"`
+  in `log/development.log`, and no `SECRET` string anywhere in the log. Legacy
+  `authentication_test.rb` and `disabled_rest_api_test.rb` unchanged and green.
+- Known limits: only Rails' own parameter logging is covered. `config/application.rb`
+  is read at boot, so a running server needs a restart to pick the change up.

module Doorkeeper
  class Engine < Rails::Engine
    initializer "doorkeeper.params.filter", after: :load_config_initializers do |app|

Verdict

APPROVE. No blocking findings. Four commits are correct, verbatim where they claim to be, RuboCop clean and green. Findings below are documentation precision and commit hygiene.

Acceptance criteria

# Criterion Status Evidence
7 ?key= logged as "key"=>"[FILTERED]" Met Live request against the running container. Log lines: Parameters: {"key"=>"[FILTERED]", "keywords"=>"plain", "id"=>"current"} and Parameters: {"bearer_token"=>"[FILTERED]", ...}.
15 Deleting a user with OAuth tokens and grants succeeds Met app/models/user.rb:105-108, test/unit/user_test.rb:403.

Verified backport claims

Every "verbatim" claim in the commit messages and architecture.md checks out against tag 6.1.4 by git blob hash:

  • app/models/user.rb at HEAD equals 6.1.4 exactly.
  • config/application.rb and test/unit/lib/parameter_filtering_test.rb at commit 0567236de equal 6.1.4 exactly. At HEAD they differ from 6.1.4 only by the /\Abearer_token\z/ entry and the one appended test case.
  • Upstream provenance: #43986 is r24609, merged to 6.1-stable as r24611 (2c933137b, adds :salt, :twofa_totp_key). #44371 is r24992 (Bogdan Egikov's patch), merged as r24994 (ddd1ea49e, 2026-08-25). 6.1.4 was tagged 2026-08-26.
  • The bearer_token test cannot pass for the wrong reason: Doorkeeper's own filter in its engine covers client_secret, authentication_token, access_token, refresh_token and code only.

Blocking findings

None.

Non-blocking findings

R-9. Architecture 2.2 overclaims "no SECRET string anywhere in the log".

  • Where: ai-workflow/architecture.md, section 2.2 "Verified" bullet.
  • Problem: I repeated the experiment. A PAT-shaped value (rmpat_...) sent via ?key= or the header appears zero times in the log. But a purely alphanumeric value sent via ?key= appears once, in the SQL log of the legacy lookup:
Token Load (2.4ms)  SELECT "tokens".* FROM "tokens" WHERE "tokens"."action" = $1 AND "tokens"."value" = $2 LIMIT $3  [["action", "api"], ["value", "REVIEWSECRET..."], ["LIMIT", 1]]

Token.find_token (app/models/token.rb:116) only refuses values that fail /\A[a-z0-9]+\z/i, then queries with the plaintext as a bind value. ActiveRecord logs bind values at debug level. This is 6.1.2 behaviour for every legacy key, not introduced by this diff, and PATs escape it only because the rmpat_ prefix contains an underscore.

  • Why it matters: the README will inherit this sentence as a security claim. Also config/environments/production.rb sets no log_level, and Rails' default is debug, so this is not only a development matter for legacy keys.
  • Suggested fix: qualify the claim to "the PAT plaintext never reaches the log; legacy 40-hex keys still appear in SQL debug logging as before". Consider a README limits line. Out of scope to fix in code.

R-10. Architecture 1.3.1 gives the wrong reason a PAT misses the legacy regex.

  • Where: ai-workflow/architecture.md:215: "A 43-char base64url token fails the legacy Token.find_token regex".
  • Problem: the base64url alphabet is letters, digits, - and _. A random 43-character token is purely alphanumeric roughly a quarter of the time, so length and alphabet guarantee nothing. The guarantee is the rmpat_ prefix. Spec 4.2 l.266-267 states the conclusion correctly but relies on this line for the reason.
  • Why it matters: step 4 reasons about lookup order and non-ambiguity from this fact, and R-9 depends on it.
  • Suggested fix: reword to "the rmpat_ prefix contains _, which the regex rejects, so the legacy lookup never queries with a PAT".

R-11. D-024 and the spec still cite R-5 where R-1 is meant. Carried from round 2 (R-6). decisions.md:481,504, spec header amendment note and spec 3.3. Under D-026 this now goes to a planner session; decisions.md is append-only so a one-line correction in the next entry is the fix.

R-12. Commit subjects say "to 6.1-stable" for a branch that is not 6.1-stable.

  • Where: bffc0fb41 and 0567236de subject lines.
  • Problem: upstream's wording was copied literally. The bodies say correctly "applied to the 6.1.2 base of this branch", but the subject alone reads as if the commits target 6.1-stable. Judgement call, not a defect; if you rewrite, something like Backport r24916 from 6.1.4: fix user deletion with OAuth tokens (#44343) keeps the upstream reference and states the direction.

R-13. The working tree mixes three unrelated document changes.

  • Where: uncommitted CLAUDE.md, four role files, three agent files (D-026 process change), decisions.md (D-024, D-025, D-026), spec amendments.
  • Problem: the code commits reference D-024 and D-025, which are not in history yet. The process change (D-026) is unrelated to the PAT slice.
  • Suggested fix: commit D-024/D-025 plus the spec amendments as one docs commit, and the D-026 process change as another. Commit history is graded.

R-4 (round 1) still open by design: template text after architecture.md section 2.2. Remove at step 7.

Lens-by-lens summary

  • Spec conformance. Steps 1 and 2 match spec 3.3 and 4.3 as amended. The planned test_key_param_should_be_filtered_from_logs in 8.3 is correctly dropped as a duplicate of the upstream file.
  • Correctness. User deletion traced in round 2, unchanged. Filtering: symbols match as substrings, regexes as written, confirmed by the keywords case and by the live log lines.
  • Security. Filtering covers every query-string transport a PAT will use. See R-9 for the legacy-key SQL exposure that predates this work.
  • Redmine conventions. All files carry the GPL header and frozen string literal. The test "..." style in parameter_filtering_test.rb deviates from conventions.md but is an upstream file; D-025 records the exception and the appended case matches the file. Would a maintainer accept: yes, three of four commits are their own code.
  • Tests. ActiveSupport::TestCase, require_relative '../../test_helper' at the right depth, behaviour-level assertions. Every path has a case: key, bearer_token, password, sudo_password, salt, twofa_totp_key, and the negative keywords.
  • Backward compatibility. Identical to what 6.1.4 users run, plus one more filtered parameter name. authentication_test.rb and disabled_rest_api_test.rb green.
  • Documentation. Architecture 1.8, 2.1, 2.2 accurate except R-9 and R-10. Every revision number and hash I checked is correct.
  • Diff hygiene. git diff --check clean across the range. See R-13 for the working tree.

# A personal access token (PAT) is a Doorkeeper access token that belongs to
# no OAuth application: it is issued by its owner from "My account" and
# presented to the REST API like the legacy API key. Doorkeeper stores the
# SHA-256 of the token and hands out the plaintext once, on creation.
class PersonalAccessToken < Doorkeeper::AccessToken
  include Redmine::SafeAttributes

  TOKEN_PREFIX = 'rmpat_'
  # Allowed lifetimes in days, the same list as the password_max_age setting
  LIFETIMES = [7, 30, 60, 90, 180, 365]

  # Prepends the prefix to Doorkeeper's random token so a PAT is recognisable
  # and can never be mistaken for a legacy API key
  module TokenGenerator
    def self.generate(options={})
      TOKEN_PREFIX + Doorkeeper::OAuth::Helpers::UniqueToken.generate(options)
    end
  end

  belongs_to :user, :foreign_key => 'resource_owner_id', :inverse_of => :personal_access_tokens

  scope :personal, lambda {where(:application_id => nil)}
  scope :not_revoked, lambda {where(:revoked_at => nil)}

  # Virtual attribute fed by the form; turned into expires_in on create
  attr_reader :lifetime_days

  safe_attributes 'name', 'lifetime_days'

  validates :name, :presence => true, :length => {:maximum => 255}
  validates :name, :uniqueness => {:scope => :resource_owner_id,
                                    :conditions => -> { personal.not_revoked },
                                    :case_sensitive => false}
  validates :application_id, :absence => true
  validates :lifetime_days, :inclusion => {:in => ->(token) { PersonalAccessToken.allowed_lifetimes }},
                            :on => :create

  before_validation :set_expiry, :on => :create

  # The form posts a String; the inclusion validation compares Integers.
  # Integer(value, exception: false) returns nil for '', 'abc' or '30abc'.
  def lifetime_days=(value)
    @lifetime_days = Integer(value, exception: false)
  end

  # Lifetimes an owner may choose, capped by the admin setting (0 = no cap)
  def self.allowed_lifetimes
    cap = Setting.personal_access_token_max_lifetime.to_i
    cap > 0 ? LIFETIMES.select {|days| days <= cap} : LIFETIMES
  end

  # Records the use of an application-less token, at most once a minute,
  # without loading or validating the record (as User#update_last_login_on!)
  def self.track_use(access_token)
    return unless access_token.application_id.nil?
    return if access_token.last_used_at && access_token.last_used_at >= 1.minute.ago

    where(:id => access_token.id).update_all(:last_used_at => Time.now)
  end

  # An application-less token with no scopes grants the owner's full rights,
  # exactly like the legacy API key
  def self.full_access?(access_token)
    access_token.application_id.nil? && access_token.scopes.all.empty?
  end

  def token_generator
    TokenGenerator
  end

  private

  def set_expiry
    self.expires_in = lifetime_days.days.to_i if lifetime_days.is_a?(Integer)
  end

  def generate_token
    super
    self.token_suffix = plaintext_token.last(4)
  end
end

require_relative '../test_helper'

class PersonalAccessTokenTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  def setup
    User.current = nil
  end

  def test_should_generate_prefixed_token_and_store_sha256_hash
    token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!
    plaintext = token.plaintext_token

    assert plaintext.start_with?(PersonalAccessToken::TOKEN_PREFIX)
    assert_equal 49, plaintext.length
    assert_equal Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(plaintext), token.token
    assert_equal plaintext.last(4), token.token_suffix
    assert_nil token.application_id
  end

  def test_should_be_found_by_plaintext_token
    token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!

    assert_equal token.id, Doorkeeper::AccessToken.by_token(token.plaintext_token).id
    assert_nil Doorkeeper::AccessToken.by_token('rmpat_unknown')
  end

  def test_should_set_expires_in_from_lifetime_days
    token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!(:lifetime_days => 30)

    assert_equal 30.days.to_i, token.expires_in
    assert_equal token.created_at + 30.days, token.expires_at
  end

  def test_should_accept_lifetime_as_string_from_form
    token = PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(2), :name => 'cron', :lifetime_days => '90')

    assert token.save
    assert_equal 90, token.lifetime_days
    assert_equal 90.days.to_i, token.expires_in
  end

  def test_should_require_name
    token = PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(2), :lifetime_days => 30)

    assert !token.save
    assert_include "Name cannot be blank", token.errors.full_messages
  end

  def test_should_require_lifetime
    token = PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(2), :name => 'cron')

    assert !token.save
    assert_equal [:lifetime_days], token.errors.attribute_names
    assert_equal ["is not included in the list"], token.errors[:lifetime_days]
    assert_nil token.expires_in
  end

  def test_should_reject_unknown_lifetime
    [45, 0, -1, 'abc', '30abc', ''].each do |value|
      token = PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(2), :name => 'cron', :lifetime_days => value)

      assert !token.save, "#{value.inspect} was accepted"
      assert_equal [:lifetime_days], token.errors.attribute_names
      assert_equal ["is not included in the list"], token.errors[:lifetime_days]
    end
  end

  def test_should_reject_lifetime_above_setting_cap
    with_settings :personal_access_token_max_lifetime => 30 do
      token = PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(2), :name => 'cron', :lifetime_days => 90)

      assert !token.save
      assert_equal [:lifetime_days], token.errors.attribute_names
      assert_equal ["is not included in the list"], token.errors[:lifetime_days]
      assert PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(2), :name => 'cron', :lifetime_days => 30).save
    end
  end

  def test_allowed_lifetimes_should_respect_cap
    with_settings :personal_access_token_max_lifetime => 0 do
      assert_equal [7, 30, 60, 90, 180, 365], PersonalAccessToken.allowed_lifetimes
    end
    with_settings :personal_access_token_max_lifetime => 90 do
      assert_equal [7, 30, 60, 90], PersonalAccessToken.allowed_lifetimes
    end
    with_settings :personal_access_token_max_lifetime => 3 do
      assert_equal [], PersonalAccessToken.allowed_lifetimes
    end
  end

  def test_name_should_be_unique_among_active_tokens_of_user
    PersonalAccessToken.generate!(:user => User.find(2), :name => 'Cron')

    duplicate = PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(2), :name => 'cron', :lifetime_days => 30)
    assert !duplicate.save
    assert_include "Name has already been taken", duplicate.errors.full_messages

    assert PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(3), :name => 'Cron', :lifetime_days => 30).save

    PersonalAccessToken.find_by(:name => 'Cron', :resource_owner_id => 2).revoke
    assert duplicate.save
  end

  def test_should_not_accept_application
    application = Doorkeeper::Application.create!(
      :name => 'Test app', :redirect_uri => 'https://example.com/callback', :scopes => ''
    )
    token = PersonalAccessToken.new(:user => User.find(2), :name => 'cron', :lifetime_days => 30,
                                    :application => application)

    assert !token.save
    assert_include "Application must be blank", token.errors.full_messages
  end

  def test_should_have_no_refresh_token_and_blank_scopes
    token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!

    assert_nil token.refresh_token
    assert token.scopes.all.empty?
    assert_nil token.reload.scopes_string
  end

  def test_should_be_expired_after_lifetime
    token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!(:lifetime_days => 7)
    assert token.accessible?

    token.update_column(:created_at, 8.days.ago)
    token.reload
    assert token.expired?
    assert !token.accessible?
  end

  def test_revoke_should_set_revoked_at
    token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!

    token.revoke
    token.reload
    assert_not_nil token.revoked_at
    assert token.revoked?
    assert !token.accessible?
    assert_equal [], User.find(2).personal_access_tokens.not_revoked.ids
  end

  def test_track_use_should_write_last_used_at_and_throttle
    token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!
    assert_nil token.last_used_at

    # Doorkeeper.authenticate returns the base class, not ours
    PersonalAccessToken.track_use(Doorkeeper::AccessToken.find(token.id))
    first_use = token.reload.last_used_at
    assert_not_nil first_use

    token.update_column(:last_used_at, 30.seconds.ago)
    recent = token.reload.last_used_at
    PersonalAccessToken.track_use(Doorkeeper::AccessToken.find(token.id))
    assert_equal recent, token.reload.last_used_at

    token.update_column(:last_used_at, 2.minutes.ago)
    PersonalAccessToken.track_use(Doorkeeper::AccessToken.find(token.id))
    assert token.reload.last_used_at > 1.minute.ago
  end

  def test_track_use_should_ignore_application_tokens
    application = Doorkeeper::Application.create!(
      :name => 'Test app', :redirect_uri => 'https://example.com/callback', :scopes => ''
    )
    token = Doorkeeper::AccessToken.create!(
      :resource_owner_id => 2, :application => application, :expires_in => 3600
    )

    PersonalAccessToken.track_use(token)
    assert_nil token.reload.last_used_at
  end

  def test_full_access_should_be_true_only_for_app_less_token_with_blank_scopes
    application = Doorkeeper::Application.create!(
      :name => 'Test app', :redirect_uri => 'https://example.com/callback', :scopes => 'view_issues'
    )

    assert PersonalAccessToken.full_access?(PersonalAccessToken.generate!)
    assert !PersonalAccessToken.full_access?(
      Doorkeeper::AccessToken.create!(:resource_owner_id => 2, :application => application,
                                      :scopes => 'view_issues', :expires_in => 3600)
    )
    assert !PersonalAccessToken.full_access?(
      Doorkeeper::AccessToken.create!(:resource_owner_id => 2, :application => application,
                                      :scopes => '', :expires_in => 3600)
    )
    assert !PersonalAccessToken.full_access?(
      Doorkeeper::AccessToken.create!(:resource_owner_id => 2, :application_id => nil,
                                      :scopes => 'view_issues', :expires_in => 3600)
    )
  end
end

+  `app/models/personal_access_token.rb`, a subclass of `Doorkeeper::AccessToken`.
+  `User` gets `has_many :personal_access_tokens` scoped to `application_id IS NULL`
+  (`user.rb:103-104`). `config/settings.yml:339` declares

+  the admin UI and its label follow in step 5. Test helper
+  `PersonalAccessToken.generate!` (`test/object_helpers.rb:23`), unit tests
+  `test/unit/personal_access_token_test.rb` (17 tests) and one association test in
+  `user_test.rb`.
+- How the token is made: Doorkeeper's `before_validation :generate_token` asks
+  `token_generator` for the random part; ours (`personal_access_token.rb:86`) returns
+  the nested `TokenGenerator` module (l.33) whose `generate` prepends `rmpat_` to
+  `UniqueToken.generate`, so the plaintext is 6 + 43 = 49 chars. The base
+  `generate_token` then stores `SHA256(plaintext)` (Redmine's `hash_token_secrets`)
+  and keeps the plaintext in memory as `#plaintext_token`; our override (l.96) adds
+  `token_suffix` from the last four plaintext chars for the list page. Lookup is
+  Doorkeeper's `by_token`, which hashes and does an indexed `find_by`.
+- How expiry is set: the form's `lifetime_days` is a virtual attribute. The writer
+  (l.61) normalises with `Integer(value, exception: false)`, so `''`, `'abc'`,
+  `'30abc'` become nil and fail the same `inclusion` validation (l.54) as 0, -1 or
+  45. `set_expiry` (l.92) converts an allowed value to `expires_in` seconds;
+  Doorkeeper's `expires_at` is `created_at + expires_in`. One error message per bad
+  lifetime, as C-6 asked; the tests assert on `errors[:lifetime_days]` because the
+  attribute label `field_lifetime_days` is added with the other locale keys in step 5.

+  case-insensitive (l.50), so a revoked token's name can be reused; `application_id`
+  must be absent; `track_use` (l.73) writes `last_used_at` with `update_all`, skips

+  scopes (D-010). No refresh token: Doorkeeper's `use_refresh_token` attr is never set.

### 3.2 Model `app/models/personal_access_token.rb`

class PersonalAccessToken < Doorkeeper::AccessToken
  include Redmine::SafeAttributes

  TOKEN_PREFIX = 'rmpat_'
  LIFETIMES = [7, 30, 60, 90, 180, 365]   # days, same list as password_max_age

  belongs_to :user, :foreign_key => 'resource_owner_id'

  scope :personal, lambda {where(:application_id => nil)}
  scope :not_revoked, lambda {where(:revoked_at => nil)}

  attr_reader :lifetime_days              # virtual attribute fed by the form (C-1)

  safe_attributes 'name', 'lifetime_days'

  validates :name, :presence => true, :length => {:maximum => 255}
  validates :name, :uniqueness => {:scope => :resource_owner_id,
                                    :conditions => -> { personal.not_revoked },
                                    :case_sensitive => false}
  validates :application_id, :absence => true
  validates :lifetime_days, :inclusion => {:in => ->(t) { PersonalAccessToken.allowed_lifetimes }},
                            :on => :create
  # No separate presence validation on expires_in: it is derived from lifetime_days,
  # and a blank lifetime must yield exactly one error message (C-6).

  before_validation :set_expiry, :on => :create
  # use_refresh_token is false by default (attr_writer in the mixin); never set it.

  # Normalising writer (C-1): the form posts the String "30"; allowed_lifetimes holds
  # Integers, and `inclusion` compares with include?. Integer(value, exception: false)
  # returns nil for '', 'abc', '30abc', so those fail inclusion; 0, -1, 45 fail too.
  def lifetime_days=(value)
    @lifetime_days = Integer(value, exception: false)
  end
```

Behaviour, all to be implemented in this class (Doorkeeper base class untouched):

- `set_expiry`: `self.expires_in = lifetime_days.days.to_i` when `lifetime_days` is an
  Integer (after the writer above); otherwise leave `expires_in` nil, the inclusion
  error is the single message the user sees. `scopes` stays blank (`''`): blank = full
  access (D-010).
- `self.allowed_lifetimes`: `LIFETIMES` filtered by
  `Setting.personal_access_token_max_lifetime.to_i` when that is > 0 (keep values
  `<= cap`). If the cap is smaller than 7, the list is empty and creation is
  impossible; the form shows `text_personal_access_token_no_lifetime_available`.
- `token_generator` (instance method, overrides `access_token_mixin.rb:503`): returns
  an object whose `generate(opts)` yields
  `TOKEN_PREFIX + Doorkeeper::OAuth::Helpers::UniqueToken.generate(opts)`. The base
  `generate_token` (l.472-478) then stores `SHA256(plaintext)` and keeps the plaintext
  in `@raw_token` / `#plaintext_token`.
- `generate_token` override: `super`, then `self.token_suffix = plaintext_token.last(4)`.
- `expired?`, `revoked?`, `accessible?`, `revoke`, `expires_at` come from Doorkeeper
  (`arch 1.3.1`). Add `def active?; accessible?; end` only if a view needs the name.
- `self.track_use(access_token)`: class method taking the `Doorkeeper::AccessToken`
  found during authentication (Doorkeeper instantiates its base class, not ours).
  Returns unless `access_token.application_id.nil?`. Skips the write when
  `last_used_at` is present and `>= 1.minute.ago`; otherwise
  `where(:id => access_token.id).update_all(:last_used_at => Time.now)`. Mirrors
  `User#update_last_login_on!` (`user.rb:328-331`, D-013).
- `self.full_access?(access_token)`: `access_token.application_id.nil? &&
  access_token.scopes.all.empty?`. Used by `find_current_user`.

Doorkeeper 5.8 documents app-owned extra columns on access tokens via the
`custom_access_token_attributes` option (`config.rb:354`); we do not need the option
itself (it only forwards attributes through the OAuth flows), but its existence shows
that adding columns to `oauth_access_tokens` is an intended extension point (C-5).

*`Doorkeeper::AccessToken` is an ActiveRecord model owned by the gem. Subclassing it
without a `type` column means both classes read and write the same table; our class
adds validations and helpers, and `scope :personal` narrows queries to our rows.*
*`safe_attributes` is Redmine's whitelist for mass assignment: the controller writes
`token.safe_attributes = params[:personal_access_token]` and only listed attributes
are copied (`lib/redmine/safe_attributes.rb`).*

    # The stored refresh_token may be mapped and not available in cleartext.

    # Generates and sets the token value with the
    # configured Generator class (see Doorkeeper.config).
    #
    # @return [String] generated token value
    #
    # @raise [Doorkeeper::Errors::UnableToGenerateToken]
    #   custom class doesn't implement .generate method
    # @raise [Doorkeeper::Errors::TokenGeneratorNotFound]
    #   custom class doesn't exist
    #
    def generate_token
      self.created_at ||= Time.now.utc

      @raw_token = token_generator.generate(attributes_for_token_generator)
      secret_strategy.store_secret(self, :token, @raw_token)
      @raw_token
    end

    # Set of attributes that would be passed to token generator to
    # generate unique token based on them.
    #
    #  @return [Hash] set of attributes
    #
    def attributes_for_token_generator
      {
        resource_owner_id: resource_owner_id,
        scopes: scopes,
        application: application,
        expires_in: expires_in,
        created_at: created_at,
      }.tap do |attributes|
        if Doorkeeper.config.polymorphic_resource_owner?
          attributes[:resource_owner] = resource_owner
        end

        Doorkeeper.config.custom_access_token_attributes.each do |attribute_name|
          attributes[attribute_name] = public_send(attribute_name)
        end
      end
    end

    def token_generator
      generator_name = Doorkeeper.config.access_token_generator
      generator = generator_name.constantize

      return generator if generator.respond_to?(:generate)

      raise Errors::UnableToGenerateToken, "#{generator} does not respond to `.generate`."
    rescue NameError
      raise Errors::TokenGeneratorNotFound, "#{generator_name} not found"
    end

Lines 33-37 of app/models/personal_access_token.rb are:

module TokenGenerator
  def self.generate(options={})
    TOKEN_PREFIX + Doorkeeper::OAuth::Helpers::UniqueToken.generate(options)
  end
end

What it is. A small helper object whose only job is to produce the random plaintext of a new token. It is a Ruby module rather than a class because it is never instantiated. Doorkeeper only needs something that answers generate, so a module with one module-level method is the lightest thing that fits.

Why def self.generate. The self. prefix makes it a method on the module itself, called as TokenGenerator.generate(...), not on an instance. Doorkeeper calls the generator that way, so this is a required shape, not a style choice.

What generate does. It asks Doorkeeper's own UniqueToken.generate for the random part, which is 32 random bytes encoded as 43 URL-safe characters, and prepends the constant TOKEN_PREFIX, which is the string rmpat_. The result is the 49-character plaintext the user sees once. The options hash is whatever Doorkeeper passes in, such as the owner id and scopes. Our generator ignores it apart from forwarding, so the random part is exactly what any Doorkeeper token would get.

How Doorkeeper reaches it. When a token is saved for the first time, Doorkeeper's before_validation :generate_token callback runs. That method calls token_generator.generate(...). Line 86 of our file overrides token_generator to return this module instead of the gem's default generator. Doorkeeper then hashes whatever string came back with SHA-256 and stores only the hash. The plaintext stays in memory as plaintext_token for the one-time display.

Why the prefix matters. Two reasons, both defended in the spec and decisions log:

  • Recognisability. Secret scanners and support staff can spot an rmpat_ string as a Redmine token.
  • Separation from the legacy key. The legacy lookup in app/models/token.rb:116 rejects anything that is not purely letters and digits. The underscore in rmpat_ guarantees a PAT never passes that check, so the two lookups can never collide, and a PAT never reaches the legacy SQL query.

Why nest it inside the class. The module is only meaningful to PersonalAccessToken, and nesting lets it use TOKEN_PREFIX directly without qualifying it. It also keeps the file self-contained for Zeitwerk, Rails' autoloader, which expects one top-level constant per file.

Only one thing ever calls TokenGenerator: Doorkeeper, once, while a new token is being saved. After that the module is out of the picture. Here is the full chain, with the files involved.

1. Creation, inside save. Doorkeeper's mixin registers before_validation :generate_token, on: :create (gem file orm/active_record/mixins/access_token.rb:24). Because PersonalAccessToken inherits from Doorkeeper::AccessToken, that callback applies to our records too. It fires when the controller in step 6 calls @token.save, and today when tests call PersonalAccessToken.generate!.

2. Doorkeeper asks for a generator. The gem's generate_token (access_token_mixin.rb:472-478) does three things: sets created_at, calls token_generator.generate(attributes_for_token_generator), and hands the result to secret_strategy.store_secret. Our file overrides token_generator at line 86 to return TokenGenerator, so the gem's default generator is never consulted for a PAT. OAuth-flow tokens are unaffected because they are plain Doorkeeper::AccessToken instances and still use the gem's default.

3. The module produces the plaintext. TokenGenerator.generate returns rmpat_ plus 43 random characters. That string goes back to the gem as @raw_token.

4. Hashing. store_secret applies the strategy Redmine configured with hash_token_secrets (config/initializers/30-redmine.rb:41), so the token column receives the SHA-256 hex digest. The plaintext is never written to the database.

5. Our own override runs. Line 96 of our file redefines generate_token as super followed by self.token_suffix = plaintext_token.last(4). plaintext_token (access_token_mixin.rb:423) returns @raw_token because a hashing strategy cannot restore secrets. So the suffix column gets the last four characters for the list page, and the in-memory object still knows the plaintext.

6. One-time display, step 6. The controller reads @token.plaintext_token right after save, puts it in the flash, and redirects. On the next request the object is gone and the plaintext with it. This is the only moment the full string leaves the server.

7. Authentication, step 4. The generator plays no part here. Doorkeeper.authenticate(request) extracts the presented string, calls by_token, which runs find_by_plaintext_token (secret_storable.rb:42): hash the input with the same strategy, then find_by on the token column, which has a unique index. Because the stored value is a hash of the whole string including the prefix, the prefix is simply part of what gets hashed. Nothing strips or inspects it.

8. Where the prefix does matter at authentication time. find_current_user tries the legacy key first. Token.find_token (app/models/token.rb:116) rejects the PAT on its regex because of the underscore, returns nil without a query, and control falls through to Doorkeeper. That is the only place the prefix's shape is relied on, and it is a side effect of the string, not a use of the module.

So in one line: the module is a creation-time hook that decides what the random string looks like. Storage, lookup, expiry and revocation are all Doorkeeper's normal behaviour operating on the hash of that string.

Lines 41-42 are:

scope :personal, lambda {where(:application_id => nil)}
scope :not_revoked, lambda {where(:revoked_at => nil)}

Not a Ruby keyword. scope is an ActiveRecord class method, Rails' ORM layer. It is unrelated to "scope" in the OAuth sense (permissions on a token), which is an unfortunate name clash in this codebase. Here it means "a named, reusable piece of a database query".

What each line declares. scope :personal, ... defines a class method PersonalAccessToken.personal that returns the query WHERE application_id IS NULL. scope :not_revoked, ... defines PersonalAccessToken.not_revoked returning WHERE revoked_at IS NULL. Neither runs SQL when declared. They run when you actually iterate the result.

Why a lambda. The second argument must be a callable that builds the query fresh on each call. Wrapping it in lambda {...} delays evaluation. A bare where(...) would be evaluated once at class load, which matters for conditions involving the current time and is why Rails requires the callable form.

They chain. Because each scope returns a query object, not an array, you can combine them and keep adding conditions:

User.current.personal_access_tokens.not_revoked.order(:created_at => :desc)
PersonalAccessToken.personal.not_revoked.where(:resource_owner_id => 2)

Rails merges the pieces into one SQL statement.

Where they are used in this feature.

  • not_revoked appears in the uniqueness validation on lines 50-52. The :conditions option runs the lambda on the validation's own query, so "name must be unique" only counts live tokens of the same owner. A revoked token's name can be reused, which is D-014.
  • not_revoked will be used by the step 6 controller to list tokens and to look up a token for revocation, so a revoked id yields 404.
  • personal exists because PersonalAccessToken and Doorkeeper::AccessToken share one table with no type column. Any query starting from PersonalAccessToken must narrow to application-less rows itself. The User#personal_access_tokens association on user.rb:103 applies the same condition through its own lambda.

Rails mechanism to cite. This is the conventional ActiveRecord way to name query fragments. Redmine uses it throughout, for example scope :logged and scope :active a few lines below the associations in app/models/user.rb.

Line 45 is:

attr_reader :lifetime_days

What it does in plain Ruby. attr_reader :lifetime_days generates a one-line getter method, exactly equivalent to writing:

def lifetime_days
  @lifetime_days
end

Ruby objects keep their state in instance variables, which start with @. They are private by default. attr_reader is the standard shorthand for exposing one of them read-only. Its siblings are attr_writer (setter only) and attr_accessor (both).

Why only the reader here. The matching setter is written by hand on lines 61-63:

def lifetime_days=(value)
  @lifetime_days = Integer(value, exception: false)
end

A generated setter would store whatever it receives. This one normalises: the HTML form posts the string "30", and Integer("30", exception: false) turns it into the number 30, while "", "abc" or "30abc" become nil. The inclusion validation on line 54 then compares against a list of integers. That was critic finding C-1: without the conversion every form post would have failed validation.

Why this attribute is not a column. lifetime_days never reaches the database. It exists only between the form and the before_validation callback set_expiry (line 92), which converts it into expires_in seconds, which is the real column Doorkeeper reads. Rails calls this a virtual attribute: the model accepts it like any other attribute, so PersonalAccessToken.new(:lifetime_days => 30) and safe_attributes on line 47 work, but ActiveRecord does not know about it.

Why it needs to be declared at all. Two callers depend on a public lifetime_days method existing:

  • The inclusion validation reads the value through the getter.
  • The form helper in step 6, f.select :lifetime_days, reads the current value to preselect an option, and error_messages_for maps errors to the attribute name.

Note on attr_reader versus ActiveRecord attributes. For a real column you never write attr_reader; ActiveRecord generates getters and setters from the table schema. You only see attr_reader or attr_accessor in a model when the attribute is virtual, so its presence is a signal to a reader that the value is transient.

Neither of them is a keyword. That is the key insight, and it answers your second question too.

Ruby's real keywords are a fixed set of about forty: def, class, module, if, end, self, return, yield, lambda is not one, and so on. They are parsed by the language and cannot be redefined.

attr_reader is an ordinary method. It is defined on the class Module, and every Ruby class is an instance of Module. When Ruby reads the class body it executes each line as code, with self set to the class being defined. So line 45 is a method call: self.attr_reader(:lifetime_days), with the parentheses and receiver omitted. The method's body, written in C inside the interpreter, defines a new method on the class. It looks like a declaration only because it runs at class-definition time.

scope is the same idea, written in Ruby by the Rails team. Doorkeeper::AccessToken inherits from ActiveRecord::Base, which includes a module defining a class-level method scope(name, body). The method's implementation does something close to this, stripped of Rails' bookkeeping:

def scope(name, body)

...

Neither of them is a keyword. That is the key insight, and it answers your second question too.

Ruby's real keywords are a fixed set of about forty: def, class, module, if, end, self, return, yield, lambda is not one, and so on. They are parsed by the language and cannot be redefined.

attr_reader is an ordinary method. It is defined on the class Module, and every Ruby class is an instance of Module. When Ruby reads the class body it executes each line as code, with self set to the class being defined. So line 45 is a method call: self.attr_reader(:lifetime_days), with the parentheses and receiver omitted. The method's body, written in C inside the interpreter, defines a new method on the class. It looks like a declaration only because it runs at class-definition time.

scope is the same idea, written in Ruby by the Rails team. Doorkeeper::AccessToken inherits from ActiveRecord::Base, which includes a module defining a class-level method scope(name, body). The method's implementation does something close to this, stripped of Rails' bookkeeping:

def scope(name, body)
  singleton_class.define_method(name) do |*args|
    all.merge(body.call(*args))
  end
end

So scope :personal, lambda {...} is a plain method call that defines another method. validates, belongs_to, has_many, before_validation and Redmine's safe_attributes are all the same pattern.

Where the difference actually lies. Only in who wrote the method and where it is defined:

attr_reader scope
Defined on Module, in the interpreter ActiveRecord::Base, in the Rails gem
Available in every class classes inheriting from ActiveRecord::Base
Implemented in C Ruby

Yes, you can define your own. Redmine does exactly this. safe_attributes on line 47 of the model comes from lib/redmine/safe_attributes.rb. Because the model does include Redmine::SafeAttributes on line 26, that module's ClassMethods are added to the class, and safe_attributes 'name', 'lifetime_days' becomes callable in the class body. The recipe:

module Auditable
  def self.included(base)
    base.extend(ClassMethods)          # add class-level methods on include
  end

  module ClassMethods
    def audited(*attribute_names)
      define_method(:audited_attributes) { attribute_names }
    end
  end
end

class Widget < ApplicationRecord
  include Auditable
  audited :name, :price
end

Widget.new.audited_attributes now returns [:name, :price]. Ruby calls this metaprogramming; Rails documentation calls such methods "macros", which is the closest term to what you were thinking of as keywords. Same mechanism as attr_reader, only the author differs.

One practical consequence for reading Redmine. When a line at the top of a class looks declarative and you do not recognise it, it is a class method. Find where it is defined with a search for def <name> in the gem or in lib/, and read that method. There is no separate grammar to learn.

module Redmine
  module SafeAttributes
    def self.included(base)
      base.extend(ClassMethods)
    end

    module ClassMethods
      # Declares safe attributes
      # An optional Proc can be given for conditional inclusion
      # Example:
      #   safe_attributes 'title', 'pages'
      #   safe_attributes 'isbn', :if => {|book, user| book.author == user}
      def safe_attributes(*args)
        @safe_attributes ||= []
        if args.empty?
          if superclass.include?(Redmine::SafeAttributes)
            @safe_attributes + superclass.safe_attributes
          else
            @safe_attributes
          end
        else
          options = args.last.is_a?(Hash) ? args.pop : {}
          @safe_attributes << [args, options]
        end
      end
    end

    # Returns an array that can be safely set by user or current user
    # Example:
    #   book.safe_attributes # => ['title', 'pages']
    #   book.safe_attributes(book.author) # => ['title', 'pages', 'isbn']
    def safe_attribute_names(user=nil)
      return @safe_attribute_names if @safe_attribute_names && user.nil?
      names = []
      self.class.safe_attributes.collect do |attrs, options|
        if options[:if].nil? || options[:if].call(self, user || User.current)
          names += attrs.collect(&:to_s)
        end
      end
      names.uniq!
      @safe_attribute_names = names if user.nil?
      names
    end

    # Returns true if attr can be set by user or the current user
    def safe_attribute?(attr, user=nil)
      safe_attribute_names(user).include?(attr.to_s)
    end

    # Returns a hash with unsafe attributes removed
    # from the given attrs hash
    # Example:
    #   book.delete_unsafe_attributes({'title' => 'My book', 'foo' => 'bar'})
    #   # => {'title' => 'My book'}
    def delete_unsafe_attributes(attrs, user=User.current)
      safe = safe_attribute_names(user)
      attrs.dup.delete_if {|k, v| !safe.include?(k.to_s)}
    end

Line 47 is:

safe_attributes 'name', 'lifetime_days'

The problem it solves. A web form posts a hash of fields. The convenient thing is to copy that hash onto the model in one go, so-called mass assignment. The danger is that an attacker adds fields the form never showed. For this model that would be expires_in, scopes, application_id or resource_owner_id: a crafted POST could mint a never-expiring token for another user. Something has to whitelist which keys may arrive from the outside.

Redmine's answer. Rails' own mechanism is strong parameters, filtering in the controller. Redmine predates it and uses its own model-side whitelist, Redmine::SafeAttributes in lib/redmine/safe_attributes.rb. Line 47 is the whole declaration for this model: exactly two names may be set from request parameters.

Yes, with one refinement: validates lives in ActiveModel, a smaller library that ActiveRecord builds on. ActiveModel provides validations, error messages and attribute naming for any Ruby object; ActiveRecord adds the database layer and pulls ActiveModel in. For a model like this one the distinction does not matter in practice, but it explains why the error messages come from i18n keys under activerecord.errors.messages in config/locales/en.yml:105-125 and why plain Ruby objects in Redmine can also use validates.

What it does. validates is another class-level macro, like scope. It registers a check that runs when save, valid? or create! is called. If any check fails, save returns false, save! raises, and the reasons are collected in record.errors keyed by attribute.

The checks used in lines 49-55 of the model:

Line Validator Meaning
49 :presence => true name must not be nil or blank.
49 :length => {:maximum => 255} Matches the column limit in the migration.
50-52 :uniqueness => {...} Queries the table for another row with the same name. :scope => :resource_owner_id narrows it to the same owner. :conditions applies the personal.not_revoked scopes so revoked rows and OAuth-flow rows are ignored. :case_sensitive => false makes "Cron" and "cron" collide.
53 :absence => true application_id must be nil. The opposite of presence.
54-55 :inclusion => {:in => lambda} lifetime_days must be one of allowed_lifetimes. The lambda is called at validation time so the admin cap is read fresh. :on => :create limits it to new records.

Timing relative to callbacks. Line 57, before_validation :set_expiry, :on => :create, runs before these checks. Order in the class body does not decide that. Rails runs all before_validation callbacks, then all validators, then before_save, then the SQL.

Where the messages come from. A failed check adds a symbol such as :blank or :inclusion to errors. Rendering turns that into text by looking up activerecord.errors.messages.blank for the message and field_name or field_lifetime_days for the attribute label, which is why the spec adds field_lifetime_days to en.yml in step 5. The unit tests assert on the raw message "is not included in the list" because that label does not exist yet.

Doorkeeper adds its own. The gem's mixin declares validates :token, presence: true, uniqueness: ... (orm/active_record/mixins/access_token.rb:17). Inheritance means those run for our records too, alongside ours.

Yes. Precisely, validates is defined in ActiveModel, the validation and attribute library that ActiveRecord is built on and always includes. Any class inheriting from ActiveRecord::Base, which PersonalAccessToken does through Doorkeeper::AccessToken, gets it automatically. Nothing in Redmine or Doorkeeper defines it.

The practical consequences:

  • It is a class-level macro like scope, not a keyword. Each call registers a check that runs on save, save!, valid? and create!.
  • Failures land in record.errors, keyed by attribute, as symbols such as :blank or :inclusion. Rendering resolves them through config/locales/en.yml, under activerecord.errors.messages for the text and field_<attribute> for the label.
  • Validators inherited from Doorkeeper's mixin, for example validates :token, presence: true in the gem, run alongside the ones on lines 49-55 of our model.
  • before_validation callbacks such as set_expiry on line 57 always run before the validators, regardless of where they appear in the file.

  • Otherwise, 1.minute.ago is a Rails extension on integers returning a Time sixty seconds before now, and >= asks whether the stored time is at least that recent. If so, return without writing.

Net effect: at most one database write per token per minute, no matter how many requests arrive. This copies User#update_last_login_on! (app/models/user.rb), decision D-013.

  • Cost. The request path should not pay for validation and callback overhead on every call.
  • Correctness. The object in hand is a Doorkeeper::AccessToken; saving it would run the gem's validations but not ours, which is a confusing half-state. A targeted UPDATE sidesteps the question.

Time.now rather than Time.now.utc matches Redmine's own usage in user.rb; ActiveRecord converts to UTC on the way to the database.

Line 78: end. Closes the method.

RuboCop first. RuboCop is Ruby's standard linter and formatter, comparable to ESLint or golangci-lint. It has no runtime effect. It parses source files and applies a few hundred individual rules, each called a "cop", each with a name of the form Department/RuleName. Layout/EmptyLineAfterGuardClause is one cop in the Layout department, which deals with whitespace and line placement rather than logic.

How Redmine uses it. The configuration lives in .rubocop.yml at the repository root. It inherits .rubocop_todo.yml, a list of pre-existing violations that are excluded file by file so old code does not have to be rewritten. This cop is enabled for the whole tree and excluded only for one migration from 2008 (.rubocop_todo.yml:22-24). CI runs bundle exec rubocop --parallel in .github/workflows/linters.yml, so a violation fails the build. That is why conventions.md makes a clean RuboCop run a precondition for every commit, and why I run it in each review.

Layout/EmptyLineAfterGuardClause is one cop in the Layout department, which deals with whitespace and line placement rather than logic.

How Redmine uses it. The configuration lives in .rubocop.yml at the repository root. It inherits .rubocop_todo.yml, a list of pre-existing violations that are excluded file by file so old code does not have to be rewritten. This cop is enabled for the whole tree and excluded only for one migration from 2008 (.rubocop_todo.yml:22-24). CI runs bundle exec rubocop --parallel in .github/workflows/linters.yml, so a violation fails the build. That is why conventions.md makes a clean RuboCop run a precondition for every commit, and why I run it in each review.

What a guard clause is. A statement at the top of a method that exits early when a precondition is not met, instead of wrapping the rest of the method in an if. Lines 74 and 75 are two of them:

return unless access_token.application_id.nil?
return if access_token.last_used_at && access_token.last_used_at >= 1.minute.ago

The alternative, nested form would be:

if access_token.application_id.nil?
  unless access_token.last_used_at && access_token.last_used_at >= 1.minute.ago
    where(...).update_all(...)
  end
end

Ruby style, and Redmine's code, strongly prefers the flat form. The cop recognises a guard clause syntactically: a single-line return, raise, next, break or similar with a trailing if or unless modifier.

What the cop demands. After the last guard clause in a run, before the first line of the method's real work, there must be exactly one empty line. Consecutive guard clauses may sit together with no gap, as lines 74 and 75 do. The idea is visual: the reader sees a block of "conditions for leaving" separated from "what the method actually does". Without the blank line the update_all reads as if it might be part of the condition.

What happens if it is missing. RuboCop reports something like:

app/models/personal_access_token.rb:77:5: C: Layout/EmptyLineAfterGuardClause: Add empty line after guard clause.

C means convention severity. The build fails all the same. This cop is auto-correctable, so bundle exec rubocop -a <file> would insert the line.

Why it is worth knowing for this task. Two reasons:

  • The implementer will write more guard clauses in step 4, inside find_current_user, and in the step 6 controller. Every one needs the blank line.
  • When you read Redmine code and see a blank line that seems arbitrary after an early return, it is this rule, not a stylistic whim of the author.

How to check yourself. Run it on a single file from the container:

docker compose exec app bundle exec rubocop app/models/personal_access_token.rb

A clean run prints 1 file inspected, no offenses detected.

application scopes full_access? Meaning
none none true Core PAT: full rights of the owner.
present some false Normal OAuth token, scoped.
present none false OAuth token with no scopes: stays scoped to nothing, as Doorkeeper intends.
none some false Future scoped PAT: enforced through oauth_scope.

The last row is the forward-compatibility hook D-004 asked for. When scopes get a UI later, a PAT with scopes automatically flows through the existing enforcement, and this method needs no change.

private on line 90 changes the visibility of every instance method defined after it in the class body, so set_expiry (line 92) and generate_token (line 96) become private. Methods above it stay public.

What private means in Ruby. A private method can only be called from inside the object's own methods, with no explicit receiver. token.set_expiry from outside raises NoMethodError: private method 'set_expiry' called. Inside the class, set_expiry works. Since Ruby 2.7, self.set_expiry works too. There is no compile-time check; the rule is enforced when the call happens.

Why it is a method call, not a keyword. Like attr_reader, private is a method on Module. With no arguments it flips a switch that affects subsequent defs. It can also take names, private :set_expiry, to make specific methods private after the fact. The bare form is what Redmine uses everywhere.

Why it does not break the callbacks. before_validation :set_expiry on line 57 and Doorkeeper's before_validation :generate_token invoke the methods through Ruby's send, which ignores visibility. Rails relies on this. Making callback methods private is the conventional way to say "this is internal plumbing, do not call it directly", and app/models/user.rb does the same for remove_references_before_destroy and its neighbours.

A subtlety in this file. Doorkeeper defines generate_token as a public method in its mixin. Our override on line 96 sits under private, so in PersonalAccessToken the method becomes private while in Doorkeeper::AccessToken it stays public. Ruby allows a subclass to tighten visibility. The super call inside still reaches the gem's implementation. Callers outside the class never need it, and the callback still fires, so no behaviour is lost. RuboCop did not object.

What it does not cover. Class methods such as self.track_use and self.full_access? on lines 73 and 82 are unaffected by a bare private, which only applies to instance methods. Making a class method private takes private_class_method :name. Here both are public on purpose, because find_current_user in step 4 calls them from another class.

Two things you would see in other languages that Ruby lacks. There is no protected in the Java sense controlling subclass access; Ruby's protected means "callable with an explicit receiver only from instances of the same class". And there is nothing like a private field: instance variables such as @lifetime_days are always private to the object, which is why line 45 needed attr_reader to expose one.

The one real caller. Doorkeeper's mixin registers before_validation :generate_token, on: :create (orm/active_record/mixins/access_token.rb:24). When a new PersonalAccessToken is saved for the first time, ActiveRecord runs the callback chain and invokes generate_token on the record. It does that with send, which bypasses visibility, so private is not an obstacle. Our override on line 96 runs, calls super to get the gem's version, then sets token_suffix.

Who never calls it. Nothing else in the gem calls generate_token on an instance. The controller in step 6 will call @token.save, not @token.generate_token. Tests use PersonalAccessToken.generate! or create!, which also go through save. So making it private forecloses no legitimate use.

Why private is the right choice here. Calling it by hand would be a mistake anyway: it overwrites token with a fresh hash and, from line 97, a fresh suffix, but does not persist anything. Marking it private documents that the callback owns it. Redmine follows the same convention for callback methods across its models.

What happens if someone tries from outside.

token = PersonalAccessToken.new
token.generate_token
# NoMethodError: private method 'generate_token' called for an instance of PersonalAccessToken

The escape hatch, token.send(:generate_token), exists but is a signal of misuse, and RuboCop and reviewers treat it as such.

A wrinkle worth knowing. On a plain Doorkeeper::AccessToken the method is still public, because visibility is set per class, not inherited downward. So Doorkeeper::AccessToken.new.generate_token works while PersonalAccessToken.new.generate_token does not. Harmless, since OAuth-flow tokens are not created by hand either, but it is the kind of asymmetry a Ruby reviewer might ask about. The honest answer is that the override only needs to be reachable by the callback, and private states that.

require_relative '../../test_helper'

class Redmine::ApiTest::PersonalAccessTokenAuthenticationTest < Redmine::ApiTest::Base
  def setup
    super
    @user = User.find(2)
    @token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!(:user => @user)
    @plaintext = @token.plaintext_token
  end

  def teardown
    super
    User.current = nil
  end

  def test_should_accept_pat_as_bearer_token
    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => {'HTTP_AUTHORIZATION' => "Bearer #{@plaintext}"}
    assert_response :ok
    assert_select 'user login', :text => 'jsmith'
  end

  def test_should_accept_pat_in_api_key_header
    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => {'X-Redmine-API-Key' => @plaintext}
    assert_response :ok
    assert_select 'user login', :text => 'jsmith'
  end

  def test_should_accept_pat_as_key_parameter
    get "/users/current.xml?key=#{@plaintext}"
    assert_response :ok
    assert_select 'user login', :text => 'jsmith'
  end

  def test_should_accept_pat_as_basic_username_with_any_password
    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => credentials(@plaintext, 'X')
    assert_response :ok
    assert_select 'user login', :text => 'jsmith'
  end

  def test_should_accept_pat_as_access_token_parameter
    get "/users/current.xml?access_token=#{@plaintext}"
    assert_response :ok
    assert_select 'user login', :text => 'jsmith'
  end

  def test_should_deny_expired_pat
    @token.update_column(:created_at, 31.days.ago)

    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => {'X-Redmine-API-Key' => @plaintext}
    assert_response :unauthorized
    assert response.headers['WWW-Authenticate'].start_with?('Bearer')
    assert_include 'invalid_token', response.headers['WWW-Authenticate']
  end

  def test_should_deny_revoked_pat
    @token.revoke

    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => {'HTTP_AUTHORIZATION' => "Bearer #{@plaintext}"}
    assert_response :unauthorized
    assert response.headers['WWW-Authenticate'].start_with?('Bearer')
  end

  def test_should_deny_pat_of_locked_user
    locked = User.find(5)
    assert locked.locked?
    token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!(:user => locked)

    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => {'HTTP_AUTHORIZATION' => "Bearer #{token.plaintext_token}"}
    assert_response :unauthorized
  end

  def test_should_deny_unknown_token_on_every_transport
    unknown = 'rmpat_unknownunknownunknownunknownunknownunk'
    [
      {'HTTP_AUTHORIZATION' => "Bearer #{unknown}"},
      {'X-Redmine-API-Key' => unknown},
      credentials(unknown, 'X')
    ].each do |headers|
      get '/users/current.xml', :headers => headers
      assert_response :unauthorized
      assert_equal 'Basic realm="Redmine API"', response.headers['WWW-Authenticate']
    end
    get "/users/current.xml?key=#{unknown}"
    assert_response :unauthorized
    get "/users/current.xml?access_token=#{unknown}"
    assert_response :unauthorized
  end

  def test_legacy_api_key_should_still_work_on_every_transport
    key = Token.create!(:user => @user, :action => 'api').value

    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => {'X-Redmine-API-Key' => key}
    assert_response :ok
    get "/users/current.xml?key=#{key}"
    assert_response :ok
    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => credentials(key, 'X')
    assert_response :ok
    assert_select 'user login', :text => 'jsmith'
  end

  def test_full_access_pat_should_keep_admin_rights
    admin_token = PersonalAccessToken.generate!(:user => User.find(1))

    get '/users.xml', :headers => {'HTTP_AUTHORIZATION' => "Bearer #{admin_token.plaintext_token}"}
    assert_response :ok

    # api_key is hidden from users authorized via OAuth scopes; a full-access
    # PAT is not scoped, so it is shown as with the legacy key
    get '/users/current.json', :headers => {'HTTP_AUTHORIZATION' => "Bearer #{@plaintext}"}
    assert_response :ok
    assert_kind_of String, ActiveSupport::JSON.decode(response.body)['user']['api_key']
  end

  def test_scoped_application_token_should_not_get_admin_rights
    application = Doorkeeper::Application.create!(
      :name => 'Test app', :redirect_uri => 'https://example.com/callback', :scopes => 'view_issues'
    )
    token = Doorkeeper::AccessToken.create!(
      :resource_owner_id => 1, :application => application, :scopes => 'view_issues', :expires_in => 3600
    )

    get '/users.xml', :headers => {'HTTP_AUTHORIZATION' => "Bearer #{token.plaintext_token}"}
    assert_response :forbidden
  end

  def test_pat_should_update_last_used_at
    assert_nil @token.last_used_at

    get '/users/current.xml', :headers => {'X-Redmine-API-Key' => @plaintext}
    assert_response :ok
    assert_not_nil @token.reload.last_used_at
  end

  def test_pat_should_be_refused_when_rest_api_disabled
    with_settings :rest_api_enabled => '0' do
      get '/users/current.xml', :headers => {'HTTP_AUTHORIZATION' => "Bearer #{@plaintext}"}
      assert_response :forbidden
    end
  end
end

  # Returns the current user or nil if no user is logged in
  # and starts a session if needed
  def find_current_user
    user = nil
    unless api_request?
      if session[:user_id]
        # existing session
        user =
          begin
            User.active.find(session[:user_id])
          rescue
            nil
          end
      elsif autologin_user = try_to_autologin
        user = autologin_user
      elsif params[:format] == 'atom' && params[:key] && request.get? && accept_atom_auth?
        # ATOM key authentication does not start a session
        user = User.find_by_atom_key(params[:key])
      end
    end
    if user.nil? && Setting.rest_api_enabled? && accept_api_auth?
      if (key = api_key_from_request) && (user = User.find_by_api_key(key))
        # Legacy API key
      elsif (access_token = Doorkeeper.authenticate(request))
        # OAuth access token or personal access token
        if access_token.accessible?
          user = User.active.find_by_id(access_token.resource_owner_id)
          if user
            user.oauth_scope = access_token.scopes.all.map(&:to_sym) unless PersonalAccessToken.full_access?(access_token)
            PersonalAccessToken.track_use(access_token)
          end
        else
          doorkeeper_render_error
        end
      elsif /\ABasic /i.match?(request.authorization.to_s)
        # HTTP Basic, either username/password or API key/random
        authenticate_with_http_basic do |username, password|
          user = User.try_to_login(username, password)
          # Don't allow using username/password when two-factor auth is active
          if user&.twofa_active?
            render_error :message => 'HTTP Basic authentication is not allowed. Use API key instead', :status => 401
            return
          end

          user ||= User.find_by_api_key(username)
        end
        if user && user.must_change_password?
          render_error :message => 'You must change your password', :status => 403
          return
        end
      end
      # Switch user if requested by an admin user
      if user && user.admin? && (username = api_switch_user_from_request)
        su = User.find_by_login(username)
        if su && su.active?
          logger.info("  User switched by: #{user.login} (id=#{user.id})") if logger
          user = su
        else
          render_error :message => 'Invalid X-Redmine-Switch-User header', :status => 412
        end
      end
    end
    # store current ip address in user object ephemerally
    user.remote_ip = request.remote_ip if user
    user
  end

+### 2.4 Authentication: transports and `find_current_user` (step 4, D-010, D-012, D-013)
+
+- What: `config/initializers/30-redmine.rb:52-57` configures Doorkeeper's
+  `access_token_methods` with its three defaults followed by the legacy transports
+  (`X-Redmine-API-Key` header, `?key=`, HTTP Basic username), as two lambdas and
+  Doorkeeper's own `from_basic_authorization`.
+  `app/controllers/application_controller.rb:131-142` rewrites the API
+  branch of `find_current_user`. Tests:
+  `test/integration/api_test/personal_access_token_authentication_test.rb` (14 tests).
+- How the branch reads now: (1) a legacy key is looked up first and wins when it
+  matches; unlike 6.1.2, a non-matching value in the legacy transports no longer
+  short-circuits to 401 but falls through; (2) `Doorkeeper.authenticate(request)`
+  tries every configured transport in order and stops at the first non-blank value
+  (`oauth/token.rb:7-13`), hashes it and looks the row up; (3) an accessible token
+  loads the owner with `User.active.find_by_id`, and only then sets `oauth_scope`
+  when the token is not full access (`PersonalAccessToken.full_access?`) and
+  records the use (`track_use`, at most once a minute); an expired or revoked
+  token goes to `doorkeeper_render_error` (401 with a Bearer challenge); (4) the
+  Basic branch is unchanged. No ambiguity between the two key kinds: a PAT has
+  `_` and base64url characters, which `Token.find_token`'s `/\A[a-z0-9]+\z/i`
+  rejects, and a 40-hex legacy key hashes to nothing in `oauth_access_tokens`.
+- Why: D-010 (PAT = application-less Doorkeeper token with full access when
+  scopes are blank, so `User#admin?` and `allowed_to?` behave as with the legacy
+  key), D-012 (parity of transports with the legacy key), D-013 (last-used write
+  on the authentication path). `access_token_methods` is global, so
+  `GET /oauth/token/info` also accepts the new transports (C-4, accepted);
+  `POST /oauth/revoke` is unaffected (C-12).
+- Verified: 14 new integration tests green; whole `test/integration/api_test/`
+  directory green (371 runs); `account_controller_test`, `account_test`,
+  `sudo_mode_test` green; `zeitwerk:check` green. Live on the Docker server with a
+  freshly created admin token: Bearer, `X-Redmine-API-Key`, `?key=` and Basic
+  username all 200 on `/users/current.json`; `/users.json` (admin only) 200;
+  `api_key` present in the owner's `/users/current.json` (not authorized-by-OAuth);
+  unknown token 401 with `Basic realm="Redmine API"`; back-dated token 401 with
+  `Bearer realm="Redmine", error="invalid_token"`; `last_used_at` set after the
+  first request; `"key"=>"[FILTERED]"` in the log and no plaintext anywhere in it.
+  The locked-user guard was shown to matter (section 1.3.1 finding).
+- Known limits (all by decision, documented for the README): PATs bypass 2FA and
+  `must_change_password?` like the legacy key, including the Basic-username nuance
+  (D-021); expired/revoked and unknown tokens answer 401 with different

# frozen_string_literal: true

module Doorkeeper
  module OAuth
    class Token
      class << self
        def from_request(request, *methods)
          methods.inject(nil) do |_, method|
            method = self.method(method) if method.is_a?(Symbol)
            credentials = method.call(request)
            break credentials if credentials.present?
          end
        end

        def authenticate(request, *methods)
          if (token = from_request(request, *methods))
            access_token = Doorkeeper.config.access_token_model.by_token(token)
            if access_token.present? && Doorkeeper.config.refresh_token_enabled?
              access_token.revoke_previous_refresh_token!
            end
            access_token
          end
        end

        def from_access_token_param(request)
          request.parameters[:access_token]
        end

        def from_bearer_param(request)
          request.parameters[:bearer_token]
        end

        def from_bearer_authorization(request)
          pattern = /^Bearer /i
          header = request.authorization
          token_from_header(header, pattern) if match?(header, pattern)
        end

        def from_basic_authorization(request)
          pattern = /^Basic /i
          header = request.authorization
          token_from_basic_header(header, pattern) if match?(header, pattern)
        end

        private

        def token_from_basic_header(header, pattern)
          encoded_header = token_from_header(header, pattern)
          decode_basic_credentials_token(encoded_header)
        end

        def decode_basic_credentials_token(encoded_header)
          Base64.decode64(encoded_header).split(/:/, 2).first
        end

        def token_from_header(header, pattern)
          header.gsub(pattern, "")
        end

        def match?(header, pattern)
